speechtext:
A message from His Majesty the King was delivered by Major A. R. Thompson, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, the house standing:
Mr. Speaker, the King commands this honourable house to attend His Majesty immediately in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the house, went up to the senate chamber to attend His Maj esty.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker reported that when the house did attend His Majesty the King in the senate chamber, His Majesty was graciously pleased to give his royal assent to the following bills:
An Act respecting a certain Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America.
An Act to carry into effect the provisions of the Convention of the 15th September, 1938, providing for emergency regulation of the level of Rainy Lake and of the level of other boundary waters in the Rainy Lake watershed.
An Act to Encourage the Co-operative Marketing of Wheat.
An Act to Assist and Encourage Co-operative Marketing of Agricultural Products.
An Act to provide for the supervision and regulation of Trading in Grain Futures.
An Act to amend the Pension Act.
An Act to amend the Criminal Code.
An Act to provide for the Training of Young People to fit them for Gainful Employment.
To these bills the royal assent was pronounced by the Clerk of the Senate in the following words:
His Majesty the King doth assent to these bills.

Then the honourable the Speaker of the House of Commons addressed His Majesty the King as follows:
May it please Your Majesty:
The Commons of Canada have voted supplies required to enable the government to defray certain expenses of the public service.
In the name of the Commons I present to Your Majesty the following bill:
"An act for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service of the financial years ending the 31st March, 1939, and the 31st March, 1940, respectively."
To which bill I humbly request Your Majesty's assent.
To this bill the Clerk of the Senate, by command of His Majesty the King, did thereupon say:
His Majesty the King thanks his loyal subjects, accepts their benevolence, and assents to this bill.
After which His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious speech from the throne to both houses of parliament, as followeth:

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you sincerely for your addresses received on my arrival at Quebec. The queen and I deeply appreciate your loyal and affectionate messages.
I am very happy that my visit to Canada affords me the opportunity of meeting, in parliament assembled, the members of both houses. No ceremony could more completely symbolize the free and equal association of the nations of our commonwealth. As my father said, on the occasion of his silver jubilee, the unity of the British empire is no longer expressed by the supremacy of the time-honoured parliament that sits at Westminster. It finds expression to-day in the free association of nations enjoying common principles of government, a common attachment to ideals of peace and freedom, and bound together by a common allegiance to the crown.
The queen and I have been deeply touched by the warmth of the welcome accorded us since our arrival in Canada. We are greatly looking forward to visiting each of the provinces, and, before our return, to paying a brief visit to the United States.
It is my earnest hope that my present visit may give my Canadian people a deeper conception of their unity as a nation. I hope also that my visit to the United States will help to maintain the very friendly relations existing between that great country and the nations of the commonwealth.
These visits, like the one recently made by the queen and myself to the continent of Europe, will, w'e trust, be viewed as an expression of the spirit of our peoples which seek

His Majesty's Speech
ardently for closer friendship and better relations not only with our kith and kin but with the peoples of all nations and races.
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
May the blessing of Divine Providence rest upon your labours and upon my realm of Canada.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East), the house adjourned at 3.45 p.m.
Monday, May 22, 1939

speechtext:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:-
1. That a taxpayer (other than a company deriving income from a metalliferous mine to which section 89 of the act applies) shall be entitled to deduct from the tax that would otherwise be payable under the act amounts not exceeding in the aggregate ten per cent of capital costs actually incurred and paid in the period beginning May 1, 1939, and ending April 30, 1940, in respect of the construction, installation, betterment, replacement or extension of plant, machinery or fixed equipment during the same period, by deducting, in each of the first three fiscal years of the taxpayer after April 30, 1940, in which the taxpayer has taxable income, an amount not exceeding one-third of the aggregate amount of the deductions authorized.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As this resolution deals with the sales tax, I wish to discuss one point very briefly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this resolution deals with the income tax, but go ahead anyway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to put on record a suggestion which I have already made to the Minister of Finance. A company makes a sale on time, say three months, to a dealer and pays the sales tax on the goods sold. Then the dealer to whom the sale was made goes bankrupt and does not pay for the goods. It seems unfair that the company should lose not only the price of the goods which they would normally have received, but also the sales tax which they have paid. It has been a troublesome question, I believe, for a long time, but as we make refunds of various kinds through the Department of National Revenue-rebates of customs duties paid, for example-I think that in such cases the company should be refunded the sales tax which it has paid. It seems a reasonable request, and I am sure some way could be worked out of making the refund. I am making no criticism because I know the question has arisen under various governments ever 
since the sales tax was introduced, but I trust that the minister will give the matter his attention with a view to working out some method of making a refund in cases of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I may be in a position to say something about the matter when the amendments to the Special War Revenue Act are under consideration. All I can say at the moment is that the question is a very old one which has been up frequently during the last few years, and no government has ever considered that it should adopt the, suggestion which is now being made. The sales tax is really a tax on the person who makes the first sale. The ground usually advanced for remitting taxes on commodities is that the manufacturer is merely a collector of the tax from the first person to whom he sells the goods, and it is repeatedly urged that where he is not able to collect the tax he should not be obliged to pay it to the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But the tax is a tax on the sale of goods. A manufacturer, for example, sells one hundred dollars' worth of goods to a firm that goes bankrupt, and he pays a sales tax of eight dollars. But while technically he has sold the goods, actually there has never been a sale, because he gets paid nothing for them, and he loses not only the one hundred dollars he would have normally received but the eight dollars that he paid in sales tax. In other words he is paying sales tax on a transaction that was never completed. I do not think the justice of his claim for refund can be disputed. The company that writes me is a London company, and they claim that this occurs repeatedly where companies go into insolvency, as many have done during recent years. I do not think there can be any question as to the justice of their claim for a refund. The problem is to work out a method by which the refund can be made. I think that is the difficulty, because I do not imagine any government would question the right of a company to be remitted the sales tax on a sale that never took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can remember this
question arising ten years ago. One must bear in mind that the principle of the tax is that it applies on the first sale. Many subsequent sales of the same article may take place, and the question arises as to bankruptcy, and how far along the line one should proceed. It becomes very complicated. If the manufacturer who pays the tax collects from the person to whom the first sale was

Income War Tax Act
made, then since the tax becomes a part of the secondary sale price, should the second seller of the article come in, if such an adjustment is to be made?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The second seller collects
his money, or he would have a claim also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But when he does not?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If he does not, and he had paid the tax, I would say that any man who paid the tax and who was unable to collect it in a subsequent sale should not be called upon to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is practically impossible to follow it through.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I admit at once that there are technical difficulties. But I believe that manufacturing compafiies making a sale in the circumstances I have described and losing the price of the goods because the sale was not completed, should not have to lose the sales tax also. In justice to manufacturers or dealers who get into this position, an attempt should be made to remedy the situation.

I have two short questions
to ask on this resolution, which has to do with betterments and replacements. The minister the other day, as an illustration, said that the cost of a new baking oven would be considered capital expenditure entitling the owner to benefit by this resolution when making up his income tax at the end of the financial year. I have in mind steam boilers, in fact all factory equipment where the units of equipment are anywhere from one to a dozen, the manufacturer having in mind in the first instance that if one particular unit breaks down he will have in reserve other units which can readily be cut in. If one bake oven, for instance, breaks down, another will be ready for service. When it comes to replacing these pieces of equipment, whether it be steam boilers, bake ovens, lathes or what not, the employees in the particular factory concerned know more about the installation of the equipment than any outside contractor. When a firm-I am thinking now of a plant with a plant repair crew of some forty men-resolves to take out a unit of equipment, it will invariably use its own plant repair and maintenance gang, so-called- electricians, steam fitters, millwrights, engineers and chief engineers who are constantly replacing worn out or broken down equipment. The major item of cost in replacing a big oven or boiler is in the taking out of the old unit and getting ready to receive the
new one; and subsequently there is the cost of bringing in and finishing up the new unit. As the act stands, when a firm divides its plant maintenance and repair organization into two gangs, one of which is charged with the responsibility of renewing equipment, and capitalizes the wages earned by this section of the plant maintenance gang, the department requires it to pay sales tax on that portion of the expenditure for labour which is capitalized under the item of new equipment. In future, will that portion of the wages used in the installation of new plant be subject to sales tax?
My second question is this. In rebuilding, we will say, the same boiler, it is often necessary to bring in welders, bricklayers, and men trained in trades which are not represented in the plant's personnel. Will the sales tax have to be paid on their wages if their wages are capitalized, as they quite properly could be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must avoid, if I can, giving administrative rulings on the floor in respect to particular cases. That will be understood. One can make a general answer, however, to the type of question asked by my hon. friend. The test will be, is this a capital expenditure? If it is, everything in connection with it will be eligible under the resolution now under discussion. But it must be remembered that if labour cost otherwise chargeable as an expense against the ordinary income of the industry is used in connection with a capital expense to qualify under this section of the law, obviously these wages cannot be allowed over again as an expense. That is to say, the wages must appear either as wages with respect to the capital expenditure or as expense wages in connection with ordinary operation; they cannot appear twice.
The sales tax question does not arise on this resolution, and I shall have to leave it to my colleague the Minister of National Revenue when we reach the excise tax provisions.

I quite appreciate the answer, and I recognize that I could not expect an immediate ruling; but this is a convenient opportunity to get the representations on record.
Another question I should like to ask has to do with installation of new equipment. In almost fifty per cent of the cases a large part of the cost is made up in the incorporation of second-hand materials into the rebuilding of the unit. Where second-hand material, much of it purchased outside the factory in question, is used, will the minister give
Income War Tax Act

consideration, when he comes to deal with the administration of the act, to allowing such material to come under the heading of a capital cost chargeable to the capital section of a firm's balance sheet, and to having the statute applied in that regard in the same manner as it applies to new material?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to secondhand machinery, when we come to the terms of the bill to be based upon this resolution, it will be found that second-hand machinery is barred from the benefits of the measure, the reason being, of course, that the purchase of second-hand machinery does not create employment.
I was referring not to second-hand machinery but to second-hand construction materials-I-beams, angles, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same principle would apply, I am afraid. However, we will consider that between now and the time the bill comes down.

I stated my opposition to this resolution when I spoke on the budget debate. I wish to do it again, though I shall do so very briefly. When speaking on the budget I said that in my opinion the Minister of Finance, in his attempt to stimulate production and consumption as well, was beginning at the wrong end. I hold that opinion because I feel that if anything has been made abundantly clear during the last ten years it is that our capacity to produce has far outgrown our capacity to consume. That being so, I cannot see how we are going to overcome the evil- if you like to call it so-of over-production by increasing or facilitating the means of further production without at the same time broadening the basis of consumption.
Speaking in the budget debate I pointed out that, according to the Canadian Bank of Commerce index of production, Canada's productive capacity operated at only 69 per cent during March. In April the production level rose somewhat, but very slightly; it is now up to 70. That indicates that industry is still operating away below capacity. When he spoke on this resolution last Thursday the Minister of Finance said that he had assurance from manufacturers that the additions and improvements made to plants would not reduce employment, because modernized machinery

this is the reason which was given- would put them in a competitive position in markets in which they cannot now compete, and hence there would be greater production.
I do not believe I ever heard a greater fallacy. 
I have no doubt that the manufacturers who spoke to the Minister of Finance were quite sincere, but we should not take these assertions merely at their face value; we should examine them in the light of what we are doing and what has happened in- the past when productive capacity has increased. In a competitive trade, other things being equal, the product that can be sold the cheapest is the product that is being produced the cheapest, and the product that is produced the cheapest is, other things being equal, the product that is produced with the lowest labour cost. If a plant has been improved and1 modernized under this scheme and can successfully compete where it could not compete before, it is doing so because its costs of production have been reduced in consequence of the efficiency of its machinery. Generally speaking, production costs are reduced when the same number of workers are producing a larger quantity of goods, or a smaller number of workers the same quantity of goods. Whichever way it happens, it is clear that this result can be brought about only by the distribution of less purchasing power to the workers employed in relation to the quantity of goods produced, It follows, then, that no matter how the improvement is effected, the industry can compete successfully only by the elimination of competitors and by the production of goods for the market more cheaply than competitors can produce them. That is done in the main by the reduction of production costs-and, as I say, these costs are, generally speaking, the costs paid out to labour. While there may be a slight increase in the number of those employed, when the industry gets into production, workers will be displaced and -unemployment increased.
Another fact that should be clear by this time is that under the present methods of production and distribution the system cannot be kept going unless there is an ever-increasing stream of the values produced in industry going into new capital. That increase in capital was possible until within recent times, but it is no longer possible, and it makes no difference how hard we try to facilitate the investment of new capital in industry, we cannot do it unless we increase the consumption of the goods produced. The purpose to-day in every capital investment or in every improvement in the mechanism of production is to reduce production costs to the lowest point so as to get the largest amount of profit possible. As we increase the productivity of the machine and make its operations more and more automatic, we displace labour that could consume the products of the machine. The machines do not buy goods.

Income War Tax Act
There is something else that follows, and possibly what I have just stated is another way of saying it: Under our capitalist system we can keep industry going only by continually investing new capital. In other words, while capitalism can finance production, capitalism cannot finance consumption; because the purpose of the system itself is not to produce goods and services for the community but to produce profits for those who own the capital. That is why to-day, with a capital structure such as the world has never known before, distress and want and misery are on every hand.
At the peak of our productive capacity on this continent in 1929, in one hectic day in October of that year, some $14,000,000,000 were lost on the New York stock exchange, and in a relatively short time that loss had increased to the stupendous sum of $75,000,000,000. This loss took place and the world, the United States particularly, felt much poorer because of that loss. In reality, however, what was lost? Was any real material thing lost? Was not the capital itself, that is, the productive capacity of the mills, the factories and the mines of the United States, just as great after this eventful day in October, 1929, as it was on the day before? Of course it was. Neither productive capacity nor any material thing; neither food, clothing, shelter, nor any part of the means of production was less than it was before. The skill of the workers was the same; their capacity and willingness were the same. Well, what was lost? What was lost was something that had really never been there. It was merely fictitious value-value supposed to be there, by people who had thought there was no end to the amount of profits to be made out of the productive capital of the country.
What we are up against under the social system under which we live is the result of our habit of thinking of our capital structure not in terms of the quantity of goods and services that can be produced for the community, but in terms of the profits that can accrue to the owners of that capital. May I refer to something the Minister of Finance said on Thursday? It was in fact the only hopeful thing he said-the implication that he was not very sure of his ground. He said this resolution was an experiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
Does my hon. friend now say that he is sure of his ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would quote me instead of interpreting me; it would be better. It is always better to quote than to interpret.

Quite so. Well, let me quote what the minister said at page 4305 of Hansard:
The measure before us at the moment is designed to encourage those people to put their money to work. I am a firm believer that idle dollars mean idle men, and in doing everything we can to encourage investment in permanent industry to overtake the obsolescence of the last ten depression years.
I admit at once that this provision is experimental-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite.
Does my hon. friend say that when anything is in the experimental stage the person experimenting is certain of the results?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Read on.
It only makes it worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Read on more. It is
rather good, I think.
It is good; I liked it myself.

It is a good thing
there is something the hon. member likes.

There are many things I like, but there are things I do not like. To continue:
I say to industry: I think I know the Canadian parliament well enough to believe this, that if during the year industry large and small across Canada takes hold and demonstrates that employment can be and is being created by virtue of this tax credit, the Canadian parliament, no matter what its political complexion may be at the time, will give fair consideration to the results from the point of view of extending the term of operation of this provision if national benefit continues to result. I simply ask the committee to give this provision a chance for a year.
To me that indicates that the minister is not quite sure of his ground, but is willing to take a chance. But I maintain, as I have stated in these few remarks, that the evidence during the past ten years is proof positive that the minister's scheme in this instance will not work. We should begin to increase purchasing power so that consumers can buy the products of their labour. We should do that by removing every restriction on consumption, and one of those restrictions that should be removed is the sales tax. The minister showed by removing the sales tax on building material last year that he realizes that by removing that obstacle to consumption, consumption will be increased. It is only by removing these restrictions on the purchasing capacity of low paid workers that we can continue to make use of the capital structure that we have already built up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall not attempt to follow my hon. friend in detail through his interesting exposition of the socialist point of view with respect to capital and industry, except to say, with respect to his first mentioned objection to the measure now under discussion, in which he took the ground very strongly that any improvement in the efficiency of productive plant and machinery necessarily does harm rather than good-
No; I said unless it were followed by increase in consumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unless it were followed by increase in consumption; may I say that those arguments ring very familiar in my ears. They were the arguments which led to the Lancashire riots against the cotton gin nearly one hundred years ago. Yet the increase in consumption of cotton goods resulting from the improvement in cotton fabricating machinery undoubtedly provided very greatly enlarged employment as the years went on. The same thing can be said of the objection which followed the introduction of the linotype machine in the printing trades: we were told about the number of hand compositors who should lose their employment and their living as a result of it. But we all know that following the invention and extensive use of the linotype machine the consumption, if one may so express it, of the printed word grew to such an extent that the printing trades employed far more men than in the days of typesetting by hand. One might multiply such illustrations. However, suffice it to say that the government believe that there are industries which by modernizing, and so overcoming the handicaps of which I spoke the other day-in one case of a plant where the machinery was secondhand twenty-five years ago-can put themselves in a position to become effective competitors in certain foreign markets in which to-day they find it difficult to compete because of the more up-to-date equipment of their competitors in other countries exporting to the same market. I could give illustration after illustration of that sort. I assure my hon. friend that I have enough confidence in the business ability both of employers and of employees in industry to believe that unless industry sees that by making these improvements there will be additional opportunities of progress and prosperity for the industry, the improvements will not be made.
What does the minister mean by-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I let my hon. friend speak without interruption. I do not agree at all that an industry in Canada which is already

capable of efficiently producing more than it can find a market for, is likely to take advantage of this provision. Of course it is not for such cases. But my hon. friends in the corner always generalize; they speak as if a condition were general when in fact the situation can be clearly understood only when one is aware of particular conditions in a particular industry. I am sure there comes to the mind of every hon. member industries which could not profit by this measure because there is no opportunity for them to expand. An industry may be over-expanded already. But I am equally sure that nearly every hon. member can think of industries in respect of which this measure will stimulate a development which will be of advantage both to the industry concerned and to its workers. We cannot generalize and draw a particular conclusion from such generalities. This measure is broad enough to enable those who can see an advantage for Canadian industry and their own industry to do something worth while. Unless the opportunity is there to do something worth while, they will not embrace it; that is all.

With the notable skill which is characteristic of the Minister of Finance he selected an excellent illustration of the fact that improvements in machinery can bring about an increased volume of employment. I refer to the example of the linotype. That extension in printing machinery brought a new condition in the printing world, because a reduction in price followed; the price did not remain at its former level as in other industries, therefore we had a vast expansion of employment such as did not follow in some other industries, or at any rate did not follow to the same extent. In passing I might mention two other good illustrations of the same thing, the telephone and the automobile. Three large automobile companies, competing without monopoly, continued to lower prices and expand the use and sale of cars because one genius at the head of a large concern in the industry regarded that as the best way for the development to take place. The others followed, partly because they found that there was a new path to tread, and partly because they saw that perhaps, in the long run, more money was to be made by giving a better service at a lower price.
I desire to quote from a book which has been already cited by the Minister of Finance, namely the report of the employment commission. I rather like this volume, because it is one which seems to fit the mind and temper of anyone who chooses to quote from it. On almost any page you can get what you

want to serve your purpose. The figures T shall quote give equal support to the contention I propose to make and to the arguments the minister used to support his own contention. At page 110 I find that the income of the farmers of Canada was $1,088,000,000 in 1926. If that condition had continued during the seven years of the depression the total farm income would have been $7,616,000,000. Actually it was $4,304,000,000, a decline of $3,312,000,000 or an annual average of $473,000,000 during the depression as compared with the normal level of 1926. This was five times greater than the loss of the Canadian manufacturers, whom we are now about to support by means of a reduction in taxes; that I shall proceed to prove. In 1926, after paying for raw materials and wages, Canadian manufacturers had $837,800,000 left out of which to pay general overhead, profits, interest on bonded indebtedness and so on. In the five years of the depression, 1931, 1932, 1933, 1934 and 1935, they had an average of $746,355,000 remaining. During this period there would also be a sharp reduction in overhead charges, so that they would not have to pay out as much as formerly. The suggestion was made by the employment commission that some incentive should be provided to bring about increased investment in durable goods, particularly in the construction industry. Every high level of prosperity in Canada has been coincident with a high level of activity in our durable goods and construction industries. The hon. member could not take a worse example than the cotton industry in Great Britain. The point of view I am expressing to-day is a long way from the point of view which about seventy-five years ago led the Manchester workers to smash the machines. What prompted them to smash the machines at that time we now see almost every day. Take a street railway in any big city. Suppose it were decided to eliminate that form of transportation and to substitute buses. What would happen? You would soon find those with capital invested in the street railway getting their lawyers on the job. They would not go out and smash the buses; they have a far more polite and more efficient technique than that.
But what really happened in Great Britain in the cotton industry was this. Great Britain began manufacturing cotton with machinery when she was the only country in the world doing so. You have a situation something like this: Company A manufacturing cotton goods, company B manufacturing cotton goods-producing machinery, engines, looms, spinning jennys and so on. When company B has supplied all the machinery that can be absorbed by A in Great Britain, it is faced with one of two courses. It can either close its plants until obsolescence or depreciation calls for new machinery or it can look for markets abroad. Company B adopted the second course; it exported abroad. Well, the moment the British manufacturers of cotton machinery began to ship their machinery abroad they began to destroy the markets for British cottons. In the period between 1914 and 1925, whole cotton manufacturing plants were shipped from Great Britain to the orient. And not only the plants, but men skilled in the operation of the machines were sent to show the Chinese and the Japanese how to run the plants. The result was that in a very few years British shipments of cotton to China were cut in half, and Britain's market is only a very small part to-day of what it once was. Indeed, a board has been set up in Great Britain to advise on the scrapping of surplus cotton manufacturing machinery. The number of spindles and plants for the manufacturing of cotton has been substantially reduced.

"(c) On every gallon of the strength of proof used in any bonded manufactory in the production of vinegar, sixty cents, and so in proportion for any greater or less strength than the strength of proof and for any less quantity than a gallon;"

I suppose this change is being made in order to give Canadian producers of apple cider an opportunty to manufacture more of that product. I understand this will have the effect of increasing the cost of vinegar to a fairly large extent. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to say that the cost of vinegar to the consumer will be increased. What we expect is that there will be a much larger market than now exists for cider vinegar manufactured from low grade apples. The latest figures I have from the bureau of statistics in regard to the production of vinegar in Canada are for 1937, but they will give some indication of the situation. During that year the production of spirit vinegar amounted to 3,718,000 gallons; of cider vinegar to 1,166,000 gallons and of malt vinegar to 221,000 gallons. The object of this amendment of course is to create a larger market for apples of the type that can be used for the production of cider for the manufacture of vinegar.

Just how did the minister
arrive at this figure of 60 cents? I understand that the original brief of the horticultural council asked for $1.15, and here that figure has been practically cut in two. Does the minister consider this will be sufficient to stimulate the production of cider vinegar to the extent he hopes it will be stimulated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is true that the request of the horticultural council, representing the apple producers of the dominion, was for $1.15 per gallon. When people come to governments asking for what amounts to protection they are never modest in their requests, and certainly they have no idea of mercy toward a possible competitor in that field. I can assure my hon. friend that after working at the matter for some time with the officials of the department the figure of 60

Excise Act
cents was arrived at. Since the budget came down there has been time for those concerned all over the country to estimate the possible effects of this legislation in creating a market for low grade apples, and I have received nothing but commendation from apple producers and organizations of producers all the way across Canada. So I am inclined to the view that the figure at which we have arrived will fairly represent the object which it is sought to attain.

I should like to offer a
word of commendation and gratitude to the minister for having at last given us this assistance. The apple growers-and I speak principally for those in British Columbia-for years have endeavoured to secure this assistance in order to follow the advice which has been given by departments of agriculture for many years that they endeavour to deal with their low priced fruit and get it off the ripe market. The difficulty for some time has been that wholesalers and retailers have been sold on the desirability of spirit vinegar, but in more recent years certain producers of pickles and so on have actually desired cider vinegar as a softer vinegar, and they do not dislike the slight flavour which remains. I had a bottle of this latest cider vinegar in my hands a couple of days ago. It is absolutely clear; it looks exactly like water, and is a perfect product. Just now an hon. member referred to the cost. The extra cost of manufacturing spirit vinegar is not expected to exceed 4 cents a gallon. By the time that reaches the consumer, if it ever does, it will have very little effect on what he has to pay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We were on paragraph 1 of the resolution dealing with the amendment to the Excise Act.

Several members are
interested in this resolution, coming as they do from localities where old established manufacturers of vinegar, pickles, tomato sauces, ketchup and other such products are located. I understand that representations have been made on behalf of these manufacturers. I should like to speak on behalf of an industry which is located at Guelph, and also for the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Mc-Avity), who is absent to-day. As I understand it, these manufacturers were not made aware of the proposed changes and did not
have any opportunity of making representations. They claim that this tax will have the effect of increasing the cost to the consumer of spirit vinegar, not only in Ontario but in the prairie provinces, Quebec and northern Ontario, where cider vinegar is not acceptable or desired by the consumer. There will be an increased cost of manufactured products in which vinegar is an important component part, and in the cost of articles in which only spirit vinegar can be used. Cider vinegar is not satisfactory in many cases, because it changes the whole character of the product. This additional tax will mean that the total tax on alcohol will be 60 cents per proof gallon as against a basic alcohol cost of 38 cents per proof gallon. The tax will be far in excess of the cost of the alcohol, which in the opinion of these manufacturers is not reasonable. Another manufacturer states as follows:
The passing of such legislation indicates to us complete lack of understanding on the part of those responsible for such legislation of the basic and fundamental differences between spirit and cider vinegar. Cider vinegar is a fermented vinegar made by natural alcoholic fermentation of sweet cider into hard cider, followed by the generation of this alcohol into acetic acid. Properly manufactured, the resulting vinegar is a very satisfactory table vinegar, the acidity of which is controlled by the amount of sugar which appears to be available in the apples used. Because of the method of manufacture, the vinegar naturally contains a certain amount of organic substance other than acetic acid which does not detract from the vinegar as a table vinegar but which very definitely detracts from this vinegar if it is used for pickling or preserving purposes.
We are very large manufacturers of cider vinegar in the states but because of the above never recommended cider vinegar for pickling purposes but have always stressed the advantage of using distilled or spirit vinegar. In our own manufacturing operations, we confine ourselves to distilled and spirit vinegar in the manufacture of ketchup, pickles, etc., because it is the very best vinegar possible to use for this purpose and for this reason we would not be influenced to use cider vinegar regardless of what excise taxes or extra costs might be put on distilled vinegar.
For pickling purposes, the two vinegars are not interchangeable but are two distinct products. Placing a penalty tax on the one only tends to increase the cost of the finished products and will have no effect on the volume of this product because the other vinegar cannot be substituted for a spirit vinegar.
Spirit vinegar is made very much as whiskey is made in its preliminary steps in that a mash of grains is malted and then fermented to produce alcohol which is distilled off from the mash in the form of spirits. These spirits are properly generated into distilled vinegar by passing through large generators filled with beech wood shavings with the result that all the alcohol contained in the spirit is converted into acetic acid. Such a vinegar contains nothing but the acetic acid plus the volatile esters
Excise Act

which gives a boquet and aroma to the product. Because of the distillation process through which the vinegar is passed, all organic matter other than acetic acid is eliminated from the product which makes this vinegar an _ ideal vinegar for preserving purposes. This vinegar has a boquet and aroma of its own that is distinct from the flavour of cider vinegar and as this distilled vinegar has been used for generations for the purpose of pickling and preserving, it is not possible to substitute cider vinegar in its place without upsetting the flavour of the products in which it is used as well as interfering with the keeping qualities of the products in which cider vinegar might be used.
This increase in the tax on vinegar from 27 cents to 60 cents per gallon has come unexpectedly, and the result is that the vinegar and pickle manufacturers stand to suffer a great loss on contracts already entered into. If the government considers that from the point of view of the apple industry it is necessary and advisable that this change be made, perhaps it might be postponed until October 1, when the manufacturers begin to manufacture spirit vinegar for 1940. If this postponement were made, the manufacturers could complete their contracts without loss and would then have warning of the increase in tax which would apply for the next preserving year.

There is just a question or two I should like to ask the Minister of Finance. I believe it has been suggested that cider vinegar should be distilled and used by certain manufacturers. Would it not then come under this sixty cent tax? The Department of Agriculture prepared a memorandum, with which I believe the minister is familiar, in which it was suggested that distilled cider vinegar might be used by certain manufacturers who would not use ordinary cider vinegar. I do not .believe there are many manufacturers who use cider vinegar in their products. The minister is no doubt familiar with this report, which explains a certain commercial process in the making of cider vinegar. I believe that it will come under the sixty cent tax as well.

I have received a number of protests from radio dealers in Vancouver, and no doubt the minister has received similar communications. These dealers complain of the provision which enables individuals to bring radio sets in from the United States without the sets being subject to the general provision that electrical apparatus must be approved by the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario. I have one letter here which is along the general lines of other letters received. It reads:
Under the present set-up, our Canadian citizens are permitted to go into the United States, where they can take their cash, and 
buy radio sets at a low price, bring them into Canada, and use them in their homes. We are not permitted to sell this class of merchandise, and yet our customers can fill their needs for radios and electrical appliances, while our merchandise can stay and rot on the shelves, and we vainly endeavour to use every available method to entice our Canadian people to purchase our radios which must be sold at a higher price.
My informant maintains that the cost of production in Canada is higher because tihe radios must be approved by the hydro-electric commission. He goes on to say:
There is _ one of two things that must be done at once, either amend the statute of all merchandise having to be approved by the hydro electric power commission of Ontario, so that we can sell these radios legally, or stop the entry and use of them. We may point out also at this time, that some stringent action should be taken in regard to car radios, as there is not one per cent of said radios purchased in Canada.
The writer then goes on to give a list of eleven radio dealers in Vancouver who had to go out of business during the last year or two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The letter which the hon. member has just read deals with a matter of provincial law. A province has the right to set up standards for electrical equipment, and it may be possible that these radios are not legally operated in the province. But they do come in as far as our tariff laws are concerned.
I think this is more a matter of enforcing provincial law with respect to electrical standards. I have had similar complaints and have had to reply that provincial rights are sacred, that we could not possibly consider enacting legislation which would avoid the necessity of provincial approval of anything which is within the jurisdiction of the province.

I quite agree that the matter of standards is within the power of the province. But if, under federal legislation, individuals are allowed to bring in these radios free of duty, why should this item still be maintained in the tariff? If the rate of duty were reduced, the dealers might have some chance of competing with the United States dealers.

There is too great a discrepancy between the prices of radios in Canada and in the United States. I was under the impression that the last budget provided for some reduction in duty on radio tubes. I think it is admitted that the prices of radio sets in this country are out of all proportion. If the tariff is too high, there should be a reduction. If the tariff is not too high, there is no excuse for this discrepancy.

Customs Tariff
Personally I have never been able to understand why there should be this great difference in price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find the answer in the next two items.

Is it not a fact that our patent laws enter into the matter? Certain patent rights are controlled by Thermionics Limited, and this company has taken advantage of its rights under our patent laws to hold up the prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
remember the reference in the budget speech to the report of the tariff board in that connection. Of course the patent aspect of the matter is separated entirely from the application of the tariff laws, and I cannot here deal with that. Obviously our patent laws have international aspects of very wide implications, and the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret), who is in charge of patent matters, is now giving serious consideration to the report of the tariff board. Under items 445o and 445p we go to the extent of giving complete free listing to parts involved in the manufacture of tubes. This is done in order to create a competitive condition so far as the tariff can do so.

These tariff changes resulted from the reference to the tariff board, but It is evident from the report of the tariff board that there are no provincial regulations which affect the price of radios to any great extent. The report of the tariff board shows that the application of the Electrical Energy Act results in adding only 41 cents to the cost of a radio, and the difference in cycles between Ontario and other portions of the dominion amounts to 31 cents. So that 72 cents represents what the manufacturers claim to be the reason for the greatly increased cost of Canadian radios.
The report also shows that as between thirty-six radios of similar make in Canada and the United States the price in Canada is between 28 and 81 per cent higher. It is not so much a question of the tariff. A radio dealer told me in conversation the other day that all the tariff changes brought down in the budget represented not more than five dollars altogether in the construction of a $60 radio set. Moreover, the radio duties are helpful only so far as repairs are concerned; the radio repair man will benefit. This man told me that the reductions are wholly for the benefit of the manufacturer, because the parts factories in the United States are largely controlled by the big manufacturing concerns. So that this reduction really does not amount to very much.
It has been stated by an hon. member that the whole trouble lies in the Patent Act. The question was referred to the tariff board in February of last year, and the board reports that a combine does exist in the radio manufacturing business. There is no question about that. No one can put any other constructor on the report of the board or on the evidence presented. A combine does exist. What better evidence could be given of a combine than that these radio manufacturers tell you that if you bring in a radio from the United States they will exercise their right to demand its surrender for destruction?
The Patent Act applies not to radios alone but to any kind of electrical equipment, and the government would be justified in taking action under the Patent Act or under the combines act, when it is so evident that radio manufacturers by means of patents and royalties have been taking advantage of the Canadian radio purchaser to make him pay from 28 to 81 per cent more than the consumer on the other side of the line has to pay.	_
Last year radios were brought in from the United States, under the $100 exemption to the amount of about $640,000. It is only natural that a Canadian would cross the line to buy a radio when he can buy it for half the price over there. But that could be overcome and the benefit of giving employment to Canadians restored if the Canadian manufacturers would bring their prices down to a reasonable level and get away from paying royalties. We know by the report of the tariff board that three or four large manufacturers hold major control of the patents, and some are paying bigger royalties than others. But, I repeat, the whole trouble lies in the Patent Act. My contention is that the government itself should take the matter in hand and exercise control either through the Patent Act or through the combines act.

Is not this an instance of a Canadian industry which enjoys high protection losing work for Canadian workmen and business for Canadian dealers? In our part of the country the radio dealers were enjoying a fine business, but they are nearly out of business to-day because people living from fifty to a hundred miles away from the United States border will go over there to buy a radio.
Do you blame them when they can buy them there for half the price?

No, you cannot blame them. I have a letter from a constituent who says that looking through a
Customs Tariff

Sears Roebuck catalogue he saw a No. 32 radio tube, guaranteed for one year, selling for 71 cents, and in our little town that same tube would cost him $2.60. Can you blame a Canadian for buying in the United States? This man told me that these tubes were made by the same manufacturer, but when I tried to get proof I found that was not so. But the United States tube is guaranteed for one year while the Canadian tube is guaranteed for only three months, and I venture to say that the United States tube will last as long as the Canadian tube. We are losing the business in Canada, and our Canadian workmen are losing the work. Why do we continue this sort of thing? People are not foolish enough to go on, buying radios and tubes in Canada when they can get them so much more cheaply in the United States.

An application was
made by a radio dealer in the city of Calgary for a complete inquiry into the radio industry under the combines act, but his application was refused. I was pleased to hear the minister say that the whole question is being attended to by the government; for something surely should be done. After reading the evidence taken at the inquiry in Alberta into the radio tube and radio manufacturing industry, and the report of the tariff board and the evidence presented to it, I feel that the government should take immediate action.
I had a radio tube given to me some time ago. It was manufactured in the United States by a United States firm, imported into Canada, put into a carton by the Canadian General Electric Company, and on the carton outside were the Words "Made in Canada," although the tube itself was made in the United States. The same tube put into a Canadian carton sells at from fifty to seventy-five per cent higher than the price at which the same tube can be purchased in the United States. It is things like this which call for government action. I do not blame Canadians for going across to the United States and buying radio tubes when they can get them there at such a greatly reduced price; otherwise they would simply be paying an enhanced price to some combine in Canada. It is the same tube, but the combine in this country charges them from fifty to seventy-five per cent more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say to hon. members who are quite properly calling attention to this matter that- the report in question on tariff board reference No. 104 was received by the government just prior to the introduction of the budget. I think I can

say there was no more complicated report before us than the one referring to radios and radio tubes, for the reason that the scope of the report not only included tariff matters, with which the tariff board is primarily engaged, but they also found it necessary to call our attention to the fact that the real difficulty arises, as has been pointed out by speakers this afternoon, through the operation of the patent law.
In connection with the tariff, the board say at page 145 of their report:
The board recommends that this item be inserted in the customs tariff-
That is the item now under discussion.
-with _ the express understanding that such economies in production costs as will be effected

That is, in the manufacture of tubes, -must immediately toe reflected in the published selling price of the Canadian tube manufacturers, and that further, the basis for establishing prices to which reference has already been made, namely United States prices plus all charges, will be adopted as the yardstick by which Canadian selling prices of tubes to said manufacturers ,and dealers should be set in Canada.
Following that, the first action of the government, as soon as the budget was down and the items were provided for as recommended by the board, was that the Minister of Finance instructed the tariff board to regard the reference on radio as a continuing reference in order that there might be machinery for establishing from time to time the extent to which the passing-on process expected by the board was really being carried out. I have received assurances since then that such has been the case-since that date. I am not prepared to say that it is true with respect to every manufacturer of tubes. That, of course, is in process of investigation in the comparatively short time which has lapsed.
There are two other sides of the matter. One, of course, is the patent law side, which is under investigation by the Secretary of State at the present time. The hon. member for Souris raised the question of a combine, as did the hon. member for Calgary East. That also is now under investigation by the Minister of Labour, having regard to the aspects of the tariff board report which might indicate the desirability of some move in that connection. Some years ago,

I will give the committee an instance. Two years ago, on my way back from the United States, I bought a radio. After a while I got a letter from a firm in Bay street, Toronto, informing me that I had brought in a Silver Tone radio and must sign an affidavit that I would not use or dispose of that radio. I wrote back through a local lawyer asking for information as to what I had done wrong or in what respect I had infringed patent rights; stating that I had bought this radio from a reliable firm in the United States, that I considered I had paid, when I bought it, all the royalties which were involved, and that I had brought it into Canada according to Canadian law under the $100 exemption provision. They would not say what right I had infringed; they wrote back, " Sign that paper, or action will be taken immediately." I did not sign the paper. I wrote again, and I did not hear from them until, when I was coming to the session last year, I called at the office. I told them who I was, and that I wanted to know what I had done wrong-they had threatened me with a suit-and then they told me to forget all about it. They said, "You will not hear any more about the matter." What I want to know is, by what right do these people place the citizens of Canada in such a position? Surely one can appeal somewhere.

I hope that when the government pursues its inquiry into the radio tube business it will make an effort to retain the manufacture of tubes in Canada. I am informed on reliable authority that a certain tube manufacturer is reducing his staff. The

company here is only a branch of an organization in the United States manufacturing perhaps a thousand times as many radios, tubes and other radio parts. Naturally they can manufacture at a lower cost than can the company in Canada. Surely some common sense should be exercised in that regard. There may be a good argument for keeping men employed in certain industries, but if the Canadian people are paying many times the wages of individuals employed in additional charges that are levied by such organizations as the radio tube manufacturers, then I say the people of Canada ought to have some consideration rather than the company or a comparatively small number of employees. The question, however, is this: By what right do these people threaten any citizen? If the article is imported from the United States a royalty has already been paid to the parent organization of which the Canadian patentees are a subsidiary part, and I cannot understand why Canadians should be subjected to this treatment. I want to make another appeal to the Minister of National Revenue regarding the entry of kilts into this country. He has received many representations. A short time ago I made an appeal to him. I draw his attention to the fact, that these cannot be classified under the heading of uniforms, they come distinctly under the heading of dress. The duty of 374 per cent-I understand it works out at some 374 per cent-cannot have been placed there to protect any industry in this country. There is no industry making kilts in sufficient number in Canada, nor will there be for many years to come. They are all imported from the old country. This year those who desired to have them found it very difficult indeed, being faced with a duty of $40 on an outfit costing $100. I should like to know the reason why kilts cannot be imported without being subject to this high duty.
We did get some consideration from the last government, because when Mr. Rhodes was Minister of Finance, the national instrument known as the bagpipes was allowed to enter Canada free. province have corresponded with me about it, violently disagreeing with the suggestions made by him and pointing out that there is now established in Vancouver-I think it is Vancouver-a promising little industry manufacturing these kilts. I am not surprised at the
ignorance of the minister regarding this, but may I enlighten him a little. I have before me a book showing the colours, and I may tell him that there are 114 different tartans.
I ask him how long it will be before a little industry in Vancouver will be able to manufacture 114 different tartans. It just cannot be done. The old established manufacturers in Scotland are practically the only ones in the world who can supply them. For instance, if he were a McKinnon like his officer in front of him he would not want a Cameron or a Campbell tartan. It will be a long time before that little industry will be able to to supply 114 different tartans. We should be allowed to import them free of charge, because it would not interfere with the building up of an industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I can only say most apologetically that the very book which my hon. friend has before him illustrates the difficulty that the department of the Minister of National Revenue would have in trying to administer an item which differentiated cloth which would be identical with all other cloths except in one respect, that it had as a design one of those 114 different tartans. There is a large proportion of Scotsmen in the customs service; I am inclined to think that to police the matter adequately would require at least three representatives of every clan at every customs port, because all Scotsmen are not familiar with the tartans of all others. I know my hon. friend is a specialist in the matter and has given a great deal of study to it, but the average man does not know these things, and I am afraid that from an administrative point of view-and here I am going outside my field; it is my colleague the
Minister of National Revenue who would have the difficulty-I think that very book illustrates more plainly than anything I could say how difficult, if not utterly impossible, it would be to administer a distinction of that kind.

A tartan is something distinct in itself, it is distinct from all other cloths. Speaking about Scottish officials, we had an experience in 1934 when the bagpipes were coming in, it was a French customs officer who allowed them in free and a Scotsman who held them up.

Assistance is now being given in the research laboratories of the department as to the best methods of utilizing various fuels, coals included; the information thus obtained is available to all companies selling coal, and the companies are taking advantage of it. I would hesitate to say that the functions of the fuel board should be enlarged to include the marketing of coal for the various companies producing coal; that is essentially the business of the companies themselves. But we give them every assistance we can in analysing their

product and finding ways in. which it can be effectively used. Constant improvement is being made in the methods of utilizing coal for domestic heating and power purposes.

I appreciate what is being done already, but there are certain things which the companies themselves cannot do. For instance, some 400,000 tons of coal are provided for families on relief in Canada, and most of that relief coal in central Canada is United States coal. It is a matter of government policy. Canadian coal should be burned in relief homes, thus giving employment to Canadian miners and railway men. Relief coal supplied by Canadian governmental bodies should be Canadian coal, not coal mined outside the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: With regard to that point, which is an important one, I may say that wherever possible, Canadian coals are used for heating federal public buildings. My hon. friend appears to suggest that we should require the municipalities and provinces to use Canadian coal. We cannot do that, as I think my hon. friend upon reflection will realize. We do, however, suggest that they use Canadian coal. But if we told Alberta, for example, that they must use a certain kind of coal in heating their legislative buildings, they would promptly tell us to mind our own business; and they would be quite right in doing so.

I was referring to coal used in the homes of people on relief. In such circumstances Canadian coal should be used, but in the central part of Canada the coal used in relief homes is United States coal. Last year 400,000 tons of coal were used in relief homes and the bulk of it, in central Canada, was United States coal. We have to make up an annual deficit on our Canadian National Railways and if we used Canadian coal it would help our railways, give employment to railway men in moving the coal from east and west to central Canada, and provide employment for our miners. We could supply a good deal of that 400,000 tons.
I think the government could assist in moving
3,000,000 tons more Canadian coal than is now being used. We are bringing in

15,000,000 tons of coal from the United States every year, when it should be easy to transport Canadian coal to Canadian homes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: Under an order in council passed on November 8, 1938, additional assistance has been given to the movement of Canadian coal to the markets generally in the central provinces. It arose out of a condition of keen competition between different producing mines in the United States. As a result the price of United States coal declined considerably. It was not a case of dumping United States coal into Canada; they were offering it for sale in the central provinces of Canada upon the same basis as they were selling it in the United States; but the effect was to create a situation, I believe more or less temporary, whereunder United States coal was underselling Canadian coal on the basis of the assistance then being given through these subventions. Consequently the order in council was amended so as to increase the assistance given to Canadian production. Members of the committee will recall, I am sure, that the principle upon which the subvention is based is that Canadian coal shall be as far as possible in a competitive position with United States coal.

Another factor which is affecting the consumption of coal is an increasing use of fuel oil, not only in furnishing motor power for vessels, but in many manufacturing establishments and in private homes.

The fact evidently is that from 1928, about the first year we started to assist the coal mining industry in the hope of increasing our production-an object with which I am in hearty sympathy-the effect has not been to increase production. In fact, less Canadian coal is produced now than was produced ten years ago.
Had it not been for the subventions the production would have been a great deal less.
I do not know about that.
That is the whole point.

My hon. friend may be right as regards this policy of subventions, and personally I should like us to make every 71492-274
effort we can to stimulate the use of Canadian coal. Away back in 1918, long before I dreamed of coming to this house, I went out on a committee to investigate the coal mining industry of Alberta. At that time there was very little use of Alberta lignite in Manitoba; for the most part we were using United States anthracite. I returned from Alberta very much impressed with the quality of the coal produced there, and strongly recommended that we in Manitoba use as much Alberta coal as we could. After a number of years we were able almost entirely to supplant the use of United States coal by the Alberta product. But from the time I first gave some study to this question I could never make out why Canadian coal cost so much at the mine mouth as compared with coal of a similar grade in the United States. I understand that, for instance, coal in Nova Scotia costs somewhere round four dollars a ton at the mine mouth. If I am wrong, I hope some hon. member from that province will correct me, because I am speaking from memory of figures I obtained a number of years ago. Somewhat similar conditions, I believe, prevail in Alberta, where coal is easily mined in at any rate some of the mines. I realize that in some parts of Nova Scotia it is an expensive proposition to mine coal deep in the earth, perhaps under the ocean, and haul it to the surface.
On account of the depth.

Yet in the United States, where conditions are comparable with those in this country, coal is produced at a little more than half what it costs to produce it in Canada. I have never been able to ascertain why there should be that great differential, particularly in view of the fact that wages in the United States are rather higher than they are in the dominion.

Western bituminous coal is produced on a parity cost with United States coal where the situation is somewhat similar. But where you have very deep mines, going under the sea, as in eastern Canada', naturally it costs more to bring out the coal. The organization of those mines was undertaken at a time when not so much was known about development as is known to-day, and it has been more expensive to bring coal to the surface there than in many mines of the United States.	There you can run a
trainload of cars to the mine mouth, load the train, kick the brakes loose and let it go down to the wharf under its own momentum, without power. That situation exists in some of the states of the American union

Perhaps I did not make
myself understood. I am speaking of coal mined under similar conditions in both countries. I can understand the cost being very high in the Princess collieries, which run under the ocean bed. But take other mines, say at Stellarton and in Alberta, where they do not go very deep into the mine mouth, perhaps a few yards; they can dig coal from the side of the mountain, and the coal is taken out at once and loaded on the cars.
That is produced cheaply.

But at the mine mouth
the price of even that coal is in excess of the price of the same kind of coal produced in the United States. I am fairly correct in my facts because I have them somewhere on record. We have had the matter before the railway committee; and a satisfactory answer has not been given because it happens that the Canadian National Railways own a number of mines which they had to take over years ago when they acquired that part of the system which is owned in the United States. The officials told us the same thing in regard to the cost of coal. I am not objecting to the subventions or to assistance given the industry, but I should like to see Canadian coal made use of in Canada through some scientific means. Millions upon millions of tons of soft and hard coal are imported into Canada, and I would rather see the coal produced here for use in our homes and factories.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Production of coal in
Canada has kept fairly constant in the last eight or ten years if allowance is made for variations on account of depression in business conditions in 1938 as against 1937. That has been attributable, I believe, to the assistance given under these subventions. Taking the per capita consumption of coal in Canada, we find that twenty years ago it was roughly 4^ tons. In 1937, which was a good business year, it was 2-65 tons. The decline in the consumption of coal in Canada has been due to several causes. In the first place, there has been a decided improvement in combustion and utilization methods and, consequently, the securing of the maximum amount of heat units.
Then there is electricity.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: In the second place, there has been a wide extension of the use of electricity and gas, and a third important factor, the most important of all, in fact, has been the great increase in the use of fuel oil not only in industrial establishments, but in the heating of private homes that were formerly heated by coal. If Canadian production had declined in step with the Canadian use of coal per capita, the total production would be very much less than it is at the present time. Undoubtedly, whether the policy is sound or not, the maintenance of production in Canada has been in a large measure on account of the assistance given through the subventions.

Canadian coal.

This question alwavs comes up when we are talking about coal. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I do not know that I can completely answer that question; but, generally speaking, each dollar spent in subventions means the expenditure of three dollars in labour, freight and other items. One can only speculate on what might happen if certain theories could be put into practical effect. As I said before six o'clock, it might and probably would be possible to formulate a coal policy in Canada that would exclude all foreign coal and supply the requirements of Canadian householders, industry, and transportation from the production of Canadian coal, but that would entail a very heavy burden on the taxpayers of this country. Speaking generally, I do not think a policy of that kind could be put into effect. The United States ship into Canada at the present time a very considerable quantity of coal, and we have agreed in the recent trade agreement not to increase duties against United States coal during the life of the agreement. If we were to say at the expiration of the agreement that we were going to double or treble the duty against United States coal, that would have an effect on any new trade arrangements we might try to negotiate with the United States. Consequently one cannot consider one commodity alone, because the carrying out of a policy such as the hon. member suggests might work a serious injury to many other industries in Canada, apart altogether from the burden it would impose on the Canadian taxpayer. In framing and giving effect to a policy such as he suggests, one must consider its effect upon the whole trade of the country. Undoubtedly the paying of subventions in both the Alberta and Nova Scotia fields has resulted in a very much higher output of Canadian coal than would otherwise have been possible, and it is a nice question whether one should increase the subventions, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer, for the purpose of having more Canadian coal produced. It is a matter of opinion, and on the whole I think the policy as applied at present is the one best suited to the needs of this country.

The minister has gone
quite a way round to answer my question. I realize that the government would have tremendous difficulty in , arriving at an exact estimate of the additional number of men who would gain employment by producing 100,000 tons more of Canadian coal. But what I had in mind was this. The Minister of Labour
has a tremendous problem on his hands, that of finding employment for those who are unemployed to-day. Many of those unemployed in Canada to-day are experienced coal miners. The Minister of Labour wants to know how to get them to work again. What I suggest is that the government should look into this matter to ascertain how many more could be legitimately employed. The coal miner is an experienced workman; he needs the work; Canadian people could use the coal; and through an increase in the coal business thousands of men could be employed. I urge the government to investigate this part of the field; for I could not find in the employment commission's report that they mentioned the matter at all.
The minister suggested that to increase subventions would mean a tremendous expense to the taxpayers. Perhaps it would; but it must be remembered that the extent of the relief problem as we have it to-day involves a huge expense to the taxpayer, and if men can be put to work, even by an increase in subventions, it would save part of the taxes which are now allotted to relief. One hon. member, speaking before recess, mentioned that the Canadian government receives by way of tariffs through the importation of coal some ten million dollars a year. The amount which is paid in subventions is not anything like ten million dollars.

Well, that is quite a substantial ' amount. I should like to point out another thing to the committee. The impression may be abroad that to increase subventions means that more money will go to the coal mining industry. That is not so. Whatever benefit the industry receives from these subventions results only from an increase in business; those who receive the direct benefits are the railways who transport the coal and the workmen who are engaged in mining the additional amount. A good many people do not understand this. They assume that the coal owners obtain the benefits in the form of a good slice of the coal subventions. That is not so; the only benefits they receive through this policy are in an increase in their business.
I do not wish to embarrass the minister, but I should like him to answer a rather delicate question. There is a widespread impression in this country that the reason why so much United States coal is imported is that Canadian capital is invested in the United States coal mining industry.

No.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: The principle upon which these payments are made is not the need of a particular company. It is to enable Nova Scotia coal to compete on even terms with foreign coal in certain areas, say in Quebec and Ontario, where the big consuming market is. I was told, and I believe the information is correct, that in some of the mines the men object to the introduction of what might foe called labour-saving devices, on the theory that it would displace labour. The subvention principle, however, as I understand it, does not necessarily depend upon efficiency of operation. The purpose is to put Canadian coal in a competitive position with imported coal.

I cannot quite understand the minister. The purpose is to put an industry in Nova Scotia in a position to compete with industries in other areas. Unless something is known about conditions in the mining area concerned, how can we know whether or not a particular industry is in a position to compete?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend how we are to determine that?
That is what I am asking the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Who is to judge as to efficiency of operation? Take the Dominion Coal company, for instance. So far as my information goes, it is efficiently operated and ably managed, but that company could not ship its coal into Ontario if it were not for the subvention. It could not compete with cheaper coal from the United States. There might be in the United States a mine just as efficiently operated as the Dominion Coal company's mines in Nova Scotia, but because of geographical conditions, Nova Scotia coal, quite as efficiently produced, could not compete with coal from the United States. The purpose of the subvention is to assist in the
freight movement of Nova Scotia coal to the districts in the central provinces and thus enable it to compete with the imported article.

When making large subventions of this kind, does the government lay down any principle under which the coal industry must operate? Is there any condition whatever as to the economy that must be practised or the wages that must be paid?
