None whatever?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: That is a matter which is purely under provincial control. Hours of work, wages and so on are matters for provincial control and legislation.

But if this dominion government proposes to make a certain grant [DOT]-call it a subvention or subsidy or anything else you like-it surely has some control over the conditions that apply in the industry, or it can cease to give the subvention. The minister cannot avoid the issue by simply stating that the dominion government has no control whatever when it makes the grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: If I understand the hon. gentleman rightly, he is suggesting that we should attach certain conditions to the payment of the subventions-conditions that will guarantee the workmen certain wages or hours of work, certain conditions of safety and all these other matters that are peculiarly and particularly subject to provincial control.

I disagree entirely with the minister in that. It is not a question of hours of labour being under provincial control; we all recognize that they are. My submission is that when this government undertakes to make a grant, it can stipulate the conditions under which the grant is given. I have in mind particularly not so much wages and hours of labour as the regularity of work, the whole question whether or not some of these mine fields should be kept open and whether a still higher subvention might not keep some others open that should be kept open. Let me read a paragraph or two which will bring the implications of this matter to the attention of the committee. I am reading from the report-
The Halifax Herald, I suppose.

If hon. gentlemen care to make a speech they are free to do so, but in the meantime I might be allowed to make my own speech. I am quoting from the Carroll report:
Your commissioners readily admit their inability correctly and accurately to dissect or untangle intricate matters of accounting, but

Legality of action, however, is one thing, and preserving and safeguarding the industry and all that that implies is quite another thing. It is therefore the considered view of your commissioners that some legislative action should be taken in regard to the powers of holding companies.
And here we pass into the large problem of how to control great corporations that control subsidiaries. In this instance I am not clear from the statement given by the minister a few minutes ago whether the control is given to the great holding company or to the subsidiary. Apparently it is given to the subsidiary.

From the very essence of the subvention method does the hon. member think it is a bonus on the coal or a subvention on production? It is on a tonnage basis that it is paid, therefore it is all to the good for the men. We should have more subventions if it were possible. The men would ask for it, not to retrench.

I am not talking about increasing or decreasing subventions; what I am getting at is the underlying principle. Apparently a subvention might be granted to a company that has no need of it, whose accounts may show a large surplus. But those accounts might be entirely cooked for all we know; so far as this government is concerned it appears to make no difference. On the other hand there are places that have been closed up, like Thorburn. A few months ago this statement was made by the secretary of the trust fund at Thorburn:
Malnutrition is prevalent; the scourge of sickness is working in our midst; children are in need of the necessities of life, clothing, bedding; in need of medicine . . . and other things than the bare necessities as supplied by the relief committee. . . .
What is the hon. member reading from?

From a statement made by Richard Cholmondeley, secretary of the trust fund for the relief of Thorburn residents. There are undoubtedly people suffering great distress in the coal mining areas

of Nova Scotia. It may be, as some have said, that there are too many miners; that some of these mines, the less profitable, should be closed. I am not an expert in that matter. But what I suggest is that the policy which apparently has been adopted in this house for some years takes no account of the actual conditions. It may be that we are paying subsidies where no subsidies are needed. It may be that these subsidies are keeping higher cost mines in operation, or if mines are put out of operation, that apparently nothing is done for the miners at those abandoned mines. Let me repeat, I should like to know from the minister whether he has considered the advisability of controlling mining areas where subventions are being paid. I admit that hours and conditions of labour and wages come under provincial jurisdiction. But as soon as the dominion government enters the scene by making grants, surely it has a right to say under what conditions these grants will be made.
Suppose the companies do not accept the conditions; the miners would get no benefit.

Well, that is another
matter.
That is the whole thing.

But the point is that we have not yet had from the minister any statement as to whether or not there is any examination of the conditions. We do not know whether the subvention policy is working to the advantage of the miners or not. The money may be going simply to a few of these companies. I submit that we ought not merely to continue to make grants of this kind without knowing something of the conditions and the far-reaching effects which may be produced.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I do not think the argument of the hon. member is sound. There might be a coal company in Nova Scotia that was earning good profits, and we might say:	"Well, your financial statement last

They would simply say: "Very well, we are not going to sell coal in Montreal or Ontario at a loss; we will not produce the coal." The result would be that the mines would partly shut down and men would be thrown out of work. The subvention assistance is in reality by way of paying a portion of the freight on the movement of that coal. The whole purpose of the subvention when first introduced

was to enable the mines to operate at greater production, give more employment to labour and relieve unemployment. The policy may have been a wise one or a foolish one, but that is the principle upon which it was based.

speechtext: I do not know what information my hon. friend wants.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The cost of producing coal in these mines is available to the fuel board and is secured by that board. They know the cost of producing coal in each of these mines. But I come back to the point where I think my hon. friend goes astray, that it does not matter whether a mine is operating at a profit or at a loss. It may have a first-class operating result; but if under those conditions, as my hon. friend suggests, we say to such a company: "You have 71492-2754
no need of assistance from the federal government; your financial position is sound;" the company would immediately say: "Very well, we are not going to ship coal to Montreal or Ontario points at a loss." The payment of the subvention, I repeat, enables those mines to ship coal into the central parts of Canada, to give more employment to their men and, incidentally, probably to pay better wages as well. If you shut off the subvention the mines close down and the men are out of work. I am not discussing the wisdom or otherwise of the policy, but that was the purpose when it was first adopted. The vote has been increased this year in order to carry it out as has been done for several years past. Conditions in the United States mines have been such during the past eight to twelve months, so far as our information goes, that they have been producing coal at a loss for the time being. A mine in Pennsylvania or West Virginia would be quite willing to enter into a contract at a low rate to supply an Ontario industrial establishment with coal for twelve months. On the basis of the subventions as they existed under last year's vote, Nova Scotia would have lost the business. We had to step up the amount of assistance in order to enable Nova Scotia mines to retain that business and prevent an increase of unemployment among the miners of that province.

It is not my intention to discuss Nova Scotia coal, but I am satisfied that if the subventions should be withdrawn thousands of men in that province would be out of employment.
I want to discuss for a few moments the coal mines of New Brunswick. We have a small area known as the Minto district which has been producing coal for many years. In November of last year the situation there became so bad that, as I think the minister will remember, it was proposed to send a delegation here to meet the minister or the chairman of the fuel board in order to discuss conditions. The chairman of the fuel board at that time recommended that a brief be submitted pointing out the conditions that existed in that area. This was done; a comprehensive brief was prepared, which has been before the fuel board for some time, although I am sorry to say that as yet there has been no result.
The Minto area, while small compared with coal areas in Nova Scotia and perhaps in other parts of Canada, had quite a thriving industry until recently, with about 1,200 miners employed. During the worst days of the depression it was one of the better off sections in New Brunswick, but in recent
Supply-Mines-C oal

years the sale of this coal has dropped to some extent while the cost of production has increased. In 1931, to make a comparison, the producers received S4.08 a ton, while in 1937 they received only $3.38. I do not know what survey has been made in Nova Scotia along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but it is known, in this area at least, that it costs more than S3.38 to produce a ton of coal, and the operators of the area have been steadily losing on their production. Their brief is very long; it is before the minister, and I do not intend to weary the committee by reading it. In this brief the operators ask for certain things. In the first place they point out that Nova Scotia receives 32 cents a ton in subventions and other government assistance on the number of tons produced, while New Brunswick receives a total of nine cents in assistance. The Minto coal is sold principally in New Brunswick. It cannot be shipped by water but must be shipped by the two main railways, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. The cost of switching coal to the main lines is very high, and in their brief the operators ask that these switching charges be borne by the government. I think this is a reasonable request under the circumstances as outlined by them. In the second place they ask that they be given some help to enable them to ship coal to the chief consuming points in New Brunswick.	*
Those are the two principal points in the brief, and I sincerely trust that the minister and the fuel board are giving consideration to these matters. In 1938 there was a strike in the Minto area over living conditions, wages and other matters which it is not necessary to mention here. The Minister of Labour, with the assistance of the provincial government, brought about a settlement of the strike and made certain recommendations, one of which was that the operators should set up a central marketing board. I believe that has been done by the thirteen operators in that area. I believe these operators have the best interests of the miners at heart, and also that we have a fine type of miner in New Brunswick. They are of English, Irish, Scotch and French extraction, and relations between the miners and the operators have always been very good. The cost of mining coal, however, reached such heights while the price was so low that it was impossible for the operators to give the miners what they would have liked, although they have done many things. For one thing the miners wanted better school conditions, and one of the finest consolidated schools in the

province was built. The operators have also improved sanitary conditions in the area and have done much to make the living conditions of the miners better. So I would strongly urge the minister and his department to consider very carefully this question of the Minto coal area in order to see if some further assistance cannot be given these people. As I said, a subvention of 32 cents a ton is granted in Nova Scotia, which I do not consider a bit too much. I know conditions in that province; I know the difficulties that have been experienced in the mining areas; I believe ,the subventions are most necessary, and I think if they were lowered there would be increased hardship.
There was one other point I intended to mention. On the front page of the last issue of the Financial Post I noticed the statement that under the. trade treaty with the United States no increase in subventions could be made without the consent of Washington. I should like the minister to say whether the recommendations contained in the brief submitted by the operators of the Minto coal mining area have not been carried out because of the provisions of the United States treaty to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The answer to my hon.
friend's last question is in the negative. The United States treaty had and has nothing whatever to do with the situation in New Brunswick. I sympathize fully and completely with the coal industry of New Brunswick, but I think my hon. friend will admit that industry operates under certain natural handicaps.
A delegation of coal operators from New Brunswick waited on the committee of the government last January. This delegation was headed by the premier of New Brunswick, and it was urged strongly that consideration should be given to the requests contained in the brief submitted. Those requests were considered carefully, but so far we have not been able to work out a method by which we can meet them. As I recall at the moment, the chief request was that assistance should be given to the movement of coal from the Minto area to other points in New Brunswick. This request, if it were granted, would lead to many difficulties in administration. Let me remind the committee that when the subvention policy was first adopted, the aim was to put Canadian coal in a fair competitive position with United States coal. That was the chief argument put forward at the time the subvention principle was adopted.

speechtext: The minister referred to United States coal. Was not the effect of the removal of the excise tax to give assistance to United States coal as against Canadian?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I am told that amounts to about six cents a ton.

speechtext:
They have stated it

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: It is about twenty cents on anthracite and about six cents on bituminous. I was about to observe that the New Brunswick request illustrates the difficulty of applying equally and fairly the remedies intended to be provided by this subvention principle. Let me repeat that the original purpose of the introduction of subventions was to put Canadian coal in a competitive position with United States coal. Only United States coal? Was it not foreign coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The assistance given to New Brunswick coal has been given under precisely the same principle as governs the assistance given to Nova Scotia coal. It was urged by this delegation that assistance should be given to move coal from one point in New Brunswick to another point in the same province. What would have happened if that had been done? It would have meant that the government would be giving assistance to enable coal produced in the Minto district to compete with coal produced by certain mines in Nova Scotia. If this had been adopted, then the request would most likely have come from the operators in the Estevan field in Saskatchewan for assistance in moving their coal to Regina, Moose Jaw or Saskatoon in order that it might compete with coal from Alberta. Similar requests would probably have been received from the Pacific coast.
After full consideration we came to the conclusion that to adopt this principle would land us in a maze of absurdities. That is not to say that I do not sympathize fully with the operators in the Minto district. According to the information we have, and I think it is correct, the cost of mining coal in that district is rather high, and the coal is not of as good a quality as that produced in Nova Scotia. Those are the natural handicaps under which the industry in New Brunswick is operating. I repeat that I sympathize with
their situation, but as to whether or not some method can be found to give assistance which would not lead us into a maze of difficulties, I am not in position to say at the moment.

What progress has been made by the government in its negotiations with the United States government to 'bring about higher prices for coal to the consumers of Ontario. This matter is being discussed in the papers, and I should like to quote from the Financial Post of May 13, as follows:
Negotiations between Canadian and American government officials, which have been proceeding since February, are expected to bear fruit this summer in a minimum price of $5.25 a ton for bituminous coal laid down in Toronto.
As an immediate result of this price agreement, if it is achieved, the Canadian government w-ill be able to lop 75 cents a ton from the subventions paid on shipments of Nova Scotia coal to Ontario.
In other words, the suggestion is that if by negotiation you can induce the Americans to charge 75 cents more per ton, then you will be able to lop off something which you have heretofore been paying for the movement of Nova Scotia coal. The alternative is that they will be able to sell more of their coal here after we have raised the price. I am not so sure of that, and I shall leave it to my hon. friends. The article goes on:
It was all a matter of the point of view, but in the final analysis the aims of the Canadian government and those of the American producer were the same. Whatever its cause the $4.50 price in Ontario last year cost the Canadian taxpayer $1-2 million. If the price is raised to $5.25, it is estimated that it may cut the tax bill by something under $1 million, depending on when this new price becomes effective.
I would point out to my sparkling friends among the manufacturers of Ontario who have been holding the pass so long, that it is to them that the bill will be sent-they will have to pay the 75 cents. I assure my hon. friends that I personally have no regrets. I shall rejoice as I see them realizing the great benefits that come from the extension of protection from one end of this country to the other. In order to bring Nova Scotia coal up here the people of Ontario are to be made to pay a higher price for United States coal.

The discussion this evening has been most interesting. We have been shown how one of the greatest industries in Canada has had to struggle for the possession of a market. It has been brought out that about 14,000,000 tons of coal come in from the United States, about 1,000,000 tons from Wales, while Canadian production totals about 12,000,000 tons. Canada with unlimited coal supplies is furnishing only
Supply-Mines-Coal

about half the demands of the home market. This bears out what we in this corner have always maintained, that Canada is our best market. Until such time as we can adequately fill the needs of our own market, there is not much hope of a solution of this problem.
It seems to me that one of the greatest difficulties that face us is in connection with transportation. These subsidies should be given if our railroads cannot transport coal cheaply enough back and forth across this country so that our coal may be available to all sections. I realize the difficult position in which the minister finds himself. These subsidies are paid directly to the railroad companies, but the railroad companies are among the greatest Canadian investors in the Pennsylvania field. How can we expect the railroad companies to lower freight rates when both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways have such large investments in the United States fields? It is high time for a national coal policy and an investigation into this whole question to find out who owns the Canadian capital invested in United States coal mines. Then we might hope to get down to a businesslike way of handling the whole coal question. Undoubtedly we have sufficient coal resources in Canada. It is possible, as the hon. member for Macleod suggested1, that it is the railways who are benefiting from these subventions and that the workers are not getting as much as they should.
I was interested in reading a little pamphlet on a national coal policy for Canada. Speaking of the production of coal in Canada, it says at page 14:
Throughout Canada there are coal supplies estimated at twelve hundred million thousands of tons and estimated by Professor Stephen Leaeoek as sufficient to supply the dominion for thirty-six thousand years. These are truly staggering figures, and many millions of tons more than those which have given Britain the prosperity she has enjoyed during the past hundred years.
Here we are with hundreds of thousands of unemployed in Canada, and thousands of expert miners idle in the very constituency in which I live. They are sitting round the tracks with nothing to do. Yet we have millions of tons of coal in this country, and we are at present supplying only half the Canadian market. Why? Because the costs are so great. It cannot be disputed that the greatest cost of all is transportation. We have a virtual coal monopoly existing because of the two railway companies being large shareholders in coal mines in Pennsylvania; and they are the ones who claim that coal cannot be transported at a reasonable cost
[Mr. C. E. Johnston.1
from Nova Scotia or Alberta to central Canada. The conclusion seems obvious. If we suggested that they have no desire to ship Nova Scotia or Alberta coal into centra! Canada because they themselves own coal mines in the United States quite close to this country, it would not seem an unreasonable suggestion. I was indeed surprised to learn that our two railway companies are mine owners in the United States.
This little pamphlet goes on to say:
Had the provinces of Ontario and Quebec during the past thirty years taken a broad view of what was necessary for the prosperity of Canada as a whole, and had those provinces adapted themselves to using Canadian coal, much might have been done to redress the adverse trade balance, but eastern Canada blindly continued to import millions of tons of American coal, for the sake of immediate savings in expense, regardless of the fact that this was bound to make other provinces, sooner or later, unable to pay for the goods they manufactured.
Results, apparent to everyone to-day, might well have been foreseen for a number of years past, had a longer view been taken by the eastern manufacturing and financial interests, by the Canadian railways, and by the various governments from time to time in power.
I think our eastern manufacturers might well take that paragraph to heart. Ever since confederation it has been their policy to buy wherever they could at the cheapest possible price. Yet when they come to sell their manufactured goods in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and every other province they must have a protected market. When anyone speaks of raising the tariff on coal, the manufacturers have a great deal to say. Yet they are the very ones w'ho depend on the west for their markets, and I think they would be well advised to remember that the prosperity of western Canada and of the maritimes is a great factor in the prosperity of central Canada.
I was amazed when I learned that $50,000,000 a year goes out of this country to buy coal in the United States. An hon. member across the floor said that the government gets back approximately $10,000,000 in revenue, but at that, $40,000,000 goes out of Canada to buy coal. Not long ago I ran across a statement made by the Minister of Finance. On March 8 last he said that money circulated eighteen times and bank credit twenty-one times a year. If we send out of this country $50,000,000 a year for coal, a mathematician can easily figure how many billions of dollars that would mean in purchasing power if left in Canada. If we supplied our own coal requirements-and	we have ample coal
resources-and could thereby increase the

purchasing power of our people by over one billion dollars a year, surely that is well worthy of consideration. The situation calls loudly for a national fuel policy.
I believe that we should establish a quota system for coal importations, on a tonnage basis. I do not care whether the coal comes from Wales or Pennsylvania, the government would be well advised to establish a quota; and it should be sufficiently low to enable every one of our miners in the west and in the east to be put to work for a minimum of five days a week the whole year round. There is no reason why they should not work five days a week. Then if it were found that the country's full coal requirements could not be met, the deficiency could be made up by the United States. If a definite policy of that kind were adopted, the mining industry would be established on a more stable basis; they would know the requirements from year to year. As the situation is now, the mining industry does not know in what year subventions may be cut off, or in what part of the country they may be increased, thus giving an advantage to one part over another and causing disunity. We should formulate and put on the statute books a definite policy to build up our coal mining industry and give our own miners continuous employment. Then they would know that a definite quantity of coal would be required from Canadian mines each year, possibly 5,000,000 tons, and the industry would know where it stood. At the present time we are importing 15,000,000 tons of coal a year. I do not hesitate to say that our mines can produce just as efficiently as the mines in the United States. But so long as you have the two large railway companies in Canada shareholders in Pennsylvania mines, freight rates in my opinion are not going to come down to the point where it would be economic to transport coal from the east or the west to central Canada.
There is this other question, the cost of relief to the dominion government. I pointed out a moment ago that we send $50,000,000 a year outside this country for coal. Remember the statement of the Minister of Finance that money circulates eighteen times and bank credit twenty-one times a year. If we put that $50,000,000 into circulation in this country, the net result would be about one billion dollars of purchasing power, a great many more people would be put into employment. Relief expenditures would be reduced. We are spending thousands of dollars every year to take care of these people on relief. If it is necessary to give subventions, they should be
given. I believe it might save a great deal of trouble if the government would ascertain how much money the railroads have invested in the Pennsylvania fields.
I was interested in some remarks the minister made about labour-saving devices in use in the mines. A good many hon. members have from time to time ridiculed members of my own party who advocate a dividend. I should like the hon. member to tell us how we are going to get money for dividends when we have to bonus our coal to get it upon a competitive basis at all?

Let me ask the hon. member this question, and he can consult with the Minister of Mines and Resources before he answers it. Are we going to produce coal more cheaply by hand labour or modern machine methods? I think he will say, by machine methods. Then the minister has this difficulty: When he puts in modern methods to cut down the cost of producing coal so as to compete with the Pennsylvania mines, what is he going to do with the men who are displaced?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

In October and
November, 1937, steps were taken by the Department of Pensions and National Health to form a national council on nutrition. The functions of the council include: to study the nutritional status and food-consuming habits of the urban and rural population in Canada; to outline standard methods of collecting data in surveys of food consumption; to set up a nutritional standard for Canada; to interpret this nutritional standard in terms of specific foods; to determine the nutritional value of Canadian foods; to collect information regarding, and to coordinate study and research pertaining to nutrition carried out in Canada; to assemble information on dietary research carried out in other countries and to investigate the necessity and feasibility of applying the results in Canada; and when sufficient information is available, to conduct educational and publicity campaigns and by 
other means to correct unsatisfactory conditions in the dietary habits of Canadians; to collaborate in the nutrition work of the health secretariat of the League of Nations. Surveys are being carried out throughout the dominion.
I am quite in favour of making a grant of this description for this purpose, but I wondered just how the department would benefit from this expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

I do not know that the

That is just what I was hoping to hear, because it seems to me that the question of nutrition, which was discussed recently in this city by an eminent authority is one to which we should be giving attention from several points of view. Representing an agricultural constituency, I should like to see a greater amount of meat, butter and other foods used in this country. It seems to me it is all very well to make a grant of this description, but we must consider ways and means of enabling people to obtain the goods. In other words, we must endeavour to provide work with wages so that people may benefit from councils of this description and their inquiries.

I hope that some report will be made as to the effect of this income upon the people concerned, the people who are on relief, whether they are getting sufficient food or whether they are suffering from malnutrition, and if so, to what extent and for what reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We cannot do anything of that kind, I would point out, until we get money. This is the first time we have asked parliament for it.

I am prepared to vote the money; I am merely suggesting that if the money is voted we shall hope to get something for it besides a few jobs for the people who may be hired and who already may have good salaries. I am having the statement looked up. So it is not perhaps a major question. Then quite frankly there is a feeling among medical men, not only here but in the United States and to a much greater degree in Great Britain and France, that neurological cases should not be given too much attention, that you perhaps make a neurological case worse by catering -to that very disability. I know that in England and France they will not admit a neurological case at all. In the United States they have possibly gone the other way. Here is the report of the head of the Canadian pension commission:
Last October I had this whole question very carefully gone into by the medical branch, to try and find out just what hardship, if any, was being caused. A review was made of the pensioners receiving pension for functional conditions: hysteria, neuroses, psychasthenia, and so on, who saw service in France. There were 2,998 of these receiving pension at 25 per cent or less, and 1,879 above that up to 100 per cent, or a total of 4,877. The form we use to record the results of a medical examination and the rate of assessment, form 865, has two headings:	(a) entire disability, (b) pensionable
disability. In only 129 of the above cases was the pensionable disability recorded as less than the entire disability, unless there was a difference due to an organic condition. That is to say, only this small number of pensioners might possibly-I cannot say would-benefit by some such amendment.
The main source of trouble and complaint in this class of pensioner is not based upon that factor, but upon the factor of assessment. Naturally, their very disability in most eases leads them to be constantly agitating for more money. They invariably believe, or pretend to believe, that they are much more handicapped in the ordinary labour market than they actually are.
Does the minister mean [DOT] that cases of this type are not pensioned at all in Great Britain?

Mr. POAA'ER: We believe we have in the employ of the department, either as consultants on schedule of fees or as part or full-time doctors, as good neuropsychiatrists as there are in Canada, As a matter of fact our people do rate very highly in that line. The year before last a survey was made of these cases, as my hon. friend knows, and I think in almost one hundred per cent of the cases brought before the committee the findings of the departmental doctors were confirmed.

Still I would put in a plea for the man who has not only a neurological disorder but at the same time some pathological condition, quite frequently found in combination. The emotional or nervous disturbance accentuates or aggravates the pathological condition. I had a case the other day of a man with definite entitlement for sinusitis and some other disability, but these entitlements were assessed negative. He had some condition described as hysteria, and there was a conflict in the medical opinion as to whether or not that was negligible. The whole case in combination was thrown into the discard, with the net result that the community must look after the man and his family, since he is totally incapacitated. I am urging that the department should give this man neurological treatment, in view of the doubt that exists in the reports of the neuropsychiatrists; and if they cannot cure him then his disability should be assessed according to the ratio established, particularly since he saw meritorious service in a field of war.

I do not know that we can do any better than we have done. We have sent these cases to Doctor Penfield and to the Toronto psychiatry institute. I am not a medical man, as my hon. friend knows, but I do not think there ever has been a case where we have refused anything like a reasonable demand for treatment either in our hospitals by our own people or by experts outside. But I am sure my hon. friend knows of the very large number of people who just happen to have that mental slant, who are Derfectly normal in every other way but who have a fixed idea, a persecution complex, that they are not getting that to which they are entitled from the pension department, from the government, or from society. speechtext: Frankly I do not know what to do about it, except to send them to people who are specialists in that line. I am not capable of discussing this with my hon. friend or any other member of this house from the technical point of view, because I do not know enough about it.

I do not want to labour the point unduly, 'but- as the minister knows, other disabilities have a certain degree of protection under the act. If a man enlisted and served in France and later was reported to have had a pre-enlistment condition of tuberculosis, we will say, no deduction is made from his pension in respect of that fact, under certain conditions. But if a man is discharged with a neurasthenic condition, or some psychopathic condition, and it is even suspected that he had a pre-enlistment condition, he is denied that protection under the act. I am anxious to ascertain from the minister what has been done to put that man on a parity with the man suffering from another disability. Surely they could be all treated on the same basis. When the chief neuropsychiatrist says there is a constitutional defect, that diagnosis is passed on to the pension commission, and usually the man is completely out of luck so far as the protection that exists in the act is concerned. Cannot something be done to place the man with a neurological condition on the same basis as the man who had tuberculosis or some other pre-enlistment condition for which he gets protection?
I have a great deal of sympathy for many of these cases. Undoubtedly there is something in what the minister says; some men have a persecution complex, but in the majority of the cases with which I come in contact the man has an actual disability to start with. That is, he is suffering from a pathological condition as well as from some emotional or nervous disturbance which adds to his disability. His sufferings are very real; he is not a malingerer in any sense of the word, nor do I think the departmental doctors suggest that. But if he is dealt with harshly by the pension commission, and then treatment or pension is denied, so that he is not given this protection of the act, the case becomes worse and worse, and he rapidly deteriorates as his anxiety becomes greater. So I suggest to the minister that if this situation were dealt with properly and adequately, not in a hard-boiled fashion, we might satisfactorily clear up some of this difficulty. At the present moment this problem exists in almost every community, and it is a problem confronted daily by those in the community who are charged with extending aid to ex-service men in distress.

I refer to the matter of public health. I purpose spending such time as I shall take this evening in an endeavour to impress upon the government and hon. members of this committee that the lack of care is costing us annually in

this dominion numberless unnecessary deaths, and that our neglect of public health is placing us in the position of being one of the most backward nations of the world in this regard. In the last month I have been in receipt of hundreds of letters which have proved to be enlightening communications to put it mildly. As a result of the deplorable conditions which these letters indicate, and in view of the public interest that has recently been awakened about this whole question of public health, I make no apologies to the committee for discussing this matter even at this late stage of the session.
May I first remind hon. gentlemen opposite that every statement I make and every figure I use has been gathered from the best possible authority on the subject. For example, I might mention the bureau of statistics, the Canadian welfare council, the Canadian medical association, and numberless other nationally recognized organizations or individuals who are in position to issue authoritative statements.
In 1937 the national income of this country was $4,576,000,000 in round figures or, to reduce it to a figure which we can all comprehend, $411 per capita. According to an article written recently by the Hon. G. M. Weir, provincial secretary and minister of education of British Columbia, out of our national income in 1937 we spent $165,000,000 on doctors, drugs, hospitals, dentists and other health services, or S15 per person.
In recent years medical science has made magnificent strides, and it has been clearly demonstrated that a substantial proportion of this expenditure is waste. We are spending a pound for care while we spend only an ounce for prevention. For example, in Ontario in 1937, of the total expenditure of $6,000,000 in round figures for hospitals, administration, et cetera, approximately $600,000, or 10 per cent, was spent on the prevention of illness through the provincial department of national health. Thus, in my own province in 1937 the provincial government spent 90 per cent for cure and 10 per cent for prevention.
We must realize that an amazingly large proportion of our population cannot afford the cost^ of any medical attention whatsoever An additional substantial percentage cannot possibly face the expenditures of a prolonged or serious illness. To again quote the Hon. G. M. Weir:
The available evidence shows that at least one-third, or more likely one-half, of all Canadians belong to families that have incomes of less than $1,000 a year. Certainly these people can afford little or nothing for medical care. . . . Only the members of our upper income group, say 2 million to 3 million Canadians at the outside, can buy private medical care without serious difficulty.

True, we may rejoice in the advances made by medical science in recent years and that it is now possible either to cure or to immunize from many of the hitherto supposedly incurable diseases; true, we may be deeply grateful to our doctors and nurses who have given gratuitously of their services to indigent patients; true, further, we may congratulate many of our health departments, municipal centres and philanthropic organizations upon the splendid work they have done, but at the same time we cannot dodge the fact that thousands die each year in this country from preventable disease simply because we have not made these life-saving and life-giving services efficient and practically available to our population. Let me quote once again from the article to which I have referred by the Hon. G. M. Weir as follows:
Cancer killed about 12,000 Canadians in 1937. At least one-sixth of these deaths might have been prevented.
At least 550,000 persons in Canada are suffering from venereal diseases. This, in spite of the fact that syphilis, which is responsible for about 10 per cent of all insanity, and for much heart disease, blindness and infant mortality, can be practically wiped out, as Sweden has proved.
During 1936, 53,000 people were patients at some time in Canadian mental hospitals. Many of them would never have seen the inside of an institution if preventive work in mental hygiene had been adequate.
In 1937, 16.675 infants under one year of age died in Canada, or 76 per 1,000 births. With proper health services the rate need not have been higher than New Zealand's rate of 30. Thus we lost needlessly about 10,000 infant lives per year.
In 1937 more than 1,000 Canadian mothers lost their lives in childbirth. "Need Our Mothers Die?" asked the Canadian Welfare Council in a bulletin published three years ago. The answer is no-that half of our maternal deaths, or 500 a year, are preventable.
Respiratory tuberculosis took a toll of almost 5.500 lives in Canada in 1937, or 49-3 per

3.000	lives, for the tuberculosis death rate can be reduced by 50 per cent at least, as Saskatchewan's rate of only 26-5 per 100,000 in 1937 indicates.
Death rates are higher among unskilled than among professional workers. In 1931 and 1932, labourers, coal miners, metal miners, and workers in mineral-products manufacture had death rates nearly twice as high as were found among certain professional classes better able to purchase adequate medical services.

There is no more vital problem.
Let me refer to an article by one of the world's great authorities on nutrition, Sir John Boyd Orr, which appeared a short time ago in The Listener. He concludes the article in these words:
The future of a country depends not so much upon trade or wealth or even armaments, as upon the health and happiness of the people, and the physique and vigour of the race.
It must be obvious to us that twenty years from now, whether we are a vigorous, virile country, or decadent and decaying, depends directly upon the health, the care and the feeding of the expectant mothers, the nursing mothers, and the children of the present. It is appalling that we can be so blind to
this obvious fact, as is evidenced by our failure to tackle the problem in a national way. As I have said, not for a moment do I criticize the efforts, sincere, honest and efficient, that have been and are being put forward by medical health officers, philanthropic organizations, and, above all, by our doctors and nurses. The contribution that they are making is magnificent. Nor do I criticize the relief officers and officials who, in the vast majority of cases, are doing the best they can with the tools at their disposal, and under the handicap of insufficient funds to do the work they realize should and must be done. But why should it be that so large a proportion of our population who cannot afford any form of medical service whatsoever should have to depend upon either the gratuitous services of the physician, or the present limited facilities of the municipality or the province, or upon the philanthropy of well meaning citizens for their vitally necessary services? It is highly to be desired, of course, for us in this house to deal with matters of urgent importance such as unemployment, agricultural distress, defence, and other such national problems. But underneath any such consideration must be the fundamental assumption that we are dealing with a healthy, normal population. If we neglect our national health, then indeed are we paving the way toward the ultimate destruction of this nation, and it then makes little difference how we treat any other national problem.
Prior to the depression, the medical profession gratuitously and gladly served many individuals who were incapable of paying their medical bills, and the amount of free work was not excessive for any one physician. In recent years, since the depression, the need as well as the demand for gratuitous services has risen to such a degree that the majority of physicians are finding it difficult to earn even a modest living. The committee on economics of the Canadian Medical Association report that the volume of medical practice in 1932 was 63-5 per cent of the volume in 1929, and in 1932 the remunerative work was only 50 per cent as against 77-5 per cent in 1929. It is estimated that this situation has grown and is growing steadily worse.
Let it be noted, Mr. Chairman, that the unequal distribution of adequate public health services across Canada is indicated by the fact that death rates from preventable diseases in so many municipalities are much too high, and the authorities which I have consulted agree that at least one-third and maybe more of the deaths from these causes which now occur in Canada could be prevented. In the past we have boasted of our standard of living in Canada. But if we examine such figures as those I have placed upon Hansard to-night, we should be appalled at the lack of care we are taking of the health of our people and the awful wastage which has resulted and is resulting. Our record in regard to public health is by no means a proud one, to phrase it mildly. For example, in the statistics from twenty-six leading countries of the world in 1936, only four had a higher maternal death rate than had Canada, we being twenty-second in that list! Let me also draw to the attention of this committee that even though the expectation of life has been extended, the number of deaths in 1937 increased over those of 1936 by 6.800, and of this increase 2.200. or approximately one-third, were under one year of age, and 1,600, or approximately one-fourth, were between the age of one year and thirty years. In other words, we must realize that 56 per cent of the increase in deaths between 1936 and 1937 were among our children and young people under thirty years of age. We regarded it, and still do, as a ghastly tragedy that 60,000 young Canadians were killed in battle or died of wounds during the four years of the great war; and yet, in the four years from 1931 to 1934, 70,000 infants under one year of age died in Canada. Let me quote from The Lancet of June 13, 1931, page 1,279, from an article by Professor Blair Bell:
It seems almost incredible that every year one woman in every ten of those who bear children is to be more or less disabled or has

to endure an operation to cure her injuries. Yet in the absence of exact figures this seems to be a conservative estimate. Besides probably many more bear in silence minor lesions which may prove fatal later.
May I refer now to a publication of the Canadian welfare council in 1935, entitled " Need Our Mothers Die?"
Over a five year average the complete toll of motherhood in Canada in order that 230,000 children may be born is the death of 1,100 to 1,400 mothers annually, the more or less permanent handicapping of another 23,000 mothers, and the impairment of health to a lesser or greater degree of another 22,000. And the stark, unescapable condemnation of the whole unfortunate story is that at least 50 per cent of this cost is unnecessary and preventable by means within our knowledge, control and capacity, if we have but the courage and determination to apply them.
It is shockingly apparent, also, Mr. Chairman, as one reads from medical reports and journals, that at least one-third of the women who bear children receive no pre-natal care, and that upwards of 20 per cent of the pregnant women in Canada are living in circumstances that may be described as very poor.
It is notorious that malnutrition during the pregnancy period has a direct bearing on the susceptibility to septicaemia and to still births, and it therefore may be assumed without question that, as the maternal death rate in areas where concerted efforts have been made to reduce it, has been reduced, where it has remained constant is as a result of pre-natal malnutrition or undernourishment of the mother. L'Assistance Maternelle, which has done such splendid work in the city of Montreal, financed largely from private contributions, reports that:
The great number of women seeking the clinic have never heard of pre-natal care, and come only for registration, but upon explanation of its value, their cooperation for examination and in the procedures laid down has been readily obtained.
Again let me refer to the Canadian welfare council's "Need Our Mothers Die?" where I read the following quotation:
In this group of causes-*
The exceptionally bad housing conditions, together with unemployment, poverty and a low standard of living.

there would fall that percentage of maternal deaths due to impaired health generally, and arising particularly out of conditions of disease and malnourishment of the young mother in her own childhood and adolescence.
I shall quote further from that pamphlet in just a few moments. It is notorious, Mr. Chairman, that in countries such as New Zealand, Scandinavia, and Holland, malnutrition is essentially unknown. And is it not
significant that the maternal death rates in these countries are among the lowest in the world? Surely we cannot ignore the fact that the undernourished female child of today is to be the young mother of to-morrow; and if we fail to provide adequate nourishment for her, we are undermining the very foundation of the nation itself.
May I conclude these remarks with a few comments on nutrition, and then I shall make a suggestion as to the possible way in which the government might deal with this question of public health. I have in my hand an article by one who is regarded by many as the world's leading authority on nutrition, Sir John Boyd Orr. I quote:
There are other factors besides food which affect health. One of the most important of these is worry, and the psychological strain of working conditions in this mechanical age of hustle. Another important factor is bad housing. Bad housing causes both physical and moral deterioration. But there is reason to believe that the most important factor in the health and physique of children is their food.
. . . Recent tests seem to show that feeding is also an important factor in maternal mortality. All the indications are that if a diet fully adequate for health were made available to every mother and child in the country, the health and physique and the length of life of the poor would be brought nearer to the level found among the well-to-do.
In a recent interview in Toronto, Sir John referred1 to the work of Doctor E. W. McHenry, assistant professor of physiological hygiene in the Connaught laboratories of the university of Toronto. Sir John is reported as saying:
He has made a study of families in the low income group, making below $1,500 a year. And he has found that these people are eating only one-third of what they should be eating. They are not sick, but they are undernourished and when they are undernourished, he will tell you that their appetite is only three-quarters of what it should be.
Referring to the United Kingdom, and we have no reason to feel that the situation would] be any different here, Sir John Boyd Orr writes, in this article in The Listener already referred to:
It has been shown that as family income falls, the consumption of the natural foodstuffs of special health value such as fruits and vegetables, eggs, milk, butter and cheese, decreases. They show that the diet of the poorer half of the population is not up to the standard required for health, and the diet of our poorest class is so bad that it is deficient in nearly every respect.
. . . Recent scientific discoveries have revolutionized our ideas on the effect of food on health. ... The new knowledge tells us that in addition to satisfying hunger, food must contain a sufficient amount of a number of substances-about half a dozen vitamines, and about a dozen minerals-to keep the body healthy.

I cannot resist asking here if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), in the light of the figures which I have placed on Hansard tonight, will still call me "irresponsible" if I state again that "thousands have died from exposure, illness, starvation or lack of care." I wonder if the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) will still say that the one who makes such a statement is exposing himself to "ridicule." Of course my statement is true, shockingly true, and indicates that through the years there has been "lack of care" of the most priceless national asset that we have- our people.
It was a hundred years ago that a brilliant French-Canadian scientist, Savarin, stated:
The welfare of a nation depends upon the way in which it is nourished.
How true that is to-day. In many places in this dominion, as a result of lack of adequate health services, as a result of inadequate relief allowance for food, we are exposing at least one-third of our population to the perils resulting from malnutrition, preventable disease and curable disease. Surely one does not have to be dead to cease to be of value to one's country. Surely the effects of undernourishment and malnutrition undermine our nationhood as nothing else can. Surely the lack of proper available medical care is paving the way for a decadent nation.

A great deal of work is being done in many provinces in regard to cancer. In Saskatchewan cancer clinics have been established. I was startled when some years

Supply-Pensions and National Health
ago I heard a young doctor, I think Doctor Dragon, a member of the legislature, turn to the members of the legislature-there were then sixty-five of them-and tell them that in all probability thirteen of the sixty-five, if they lived up to the average, would die of cancer. It was a startling statement. That scourge is spreading.
I wish to put in a plea for just one phase of the cancer situation. Many people find it very difficult to avail themselves of the opportunities provided by the clinics, where they exist. It has been suggested to me-it is not original with me-by a woman who is interested in health work, and particularly in cancer cases, that the federal government, if it made no other contribution, might in some manner provide that people who desire to avail themselves of treatment at these cancer clinics should be provided through the federal department with free transportation to these clinics. In Saskatchewan, where distances are great and where there is a great deal of poverty at the present time, transportation is a barrier. I make this plea to the minister because it would be at least a small contribution to the splendid work that is being done in these provinces.

Is it not a fact that people who require cancer treatment at these clinics and have not the means to pay for their transportation are assisted in that way also? Are they not supplied with transportation now, to a great extent?
I understood not.
I think they are.

If that is so, it has been adopted more or less recently, for it was not the case some little time ago. I have not checked up on it lately; I have been awaiting an item of this kind, and perhaps I should have made a little further investigation. However, that does not alter the suggestion that this is a contribution which might be made by the federal government. All I wish to say is that I thoroughly endorse the position taken by the hon. member for Greenwood, and I hope that as time goes on we may see in Canada a health service for our people aimed at preventing disease, just as free and as available as education is for the children of our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I want to say just one word to thank the hon. member for Greenwood for having so eloquently placed on Hansard the result of his researches into this health question. It is a very large question. The matter of responsibility particularly is one on which it is extremely difficult to get full
agreement throughout the country. There has been no doubt at all in my mind, particularly since I have had an opportunity to give health matters that study which I have been enabled to give them since taking over this department, that the state has as much responsibility to look after the health of its citizens as it has to protect them against burglary or any other social calamity. But which particular branch of the state in Canada should do that is something not yet decided. We cannot say all at once that we are going to take over all the health services of the provinces. I am sure that if I were to decide to take over the health units in my own province we would have a kind of revolution on our hands. We would be infringing on provincial rights. The banner provincial autonomy would be raised. If other province! would follow the example of Quebec and Saskatchewan and develop their own health units it would be for the greater good of Canada.
That is the ease all along the line. There is room for cooperation. There is room for coordination of effort. There is a crying demand for some kind of conference so that we may trace, as between municipality, province and dominion, just what are our responsibilities and how we may be able to carry them out to the best of our ability in order to assist the entire population. In any event I thank the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar for their observations. I assure them that so far as I am concerned I am always glad to hear members, on whatever side of the house they may be, urge on the government and on the country that we spend more on our national health, provided that we can spend it usefully.
The minister missed the whole point of the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood.

I should like to associate myself with the observations of the two hon. gentlemen who spoke from this side of the house. At the same time I should like to point out that all pious wishes such as these probably will remain pious wishes until we find a way of getting the necessary money without added taxation or borrowing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There were three other items in the supplementaries which the committee might allow me to put through, always holding back the two items which I suggested would be held back.
Pensions branch.
629. Pension appeal court-further amount required to provide, in the event of the abolition
4388	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
of the pension appeal court, for gratuities not to exceed in any case the equivalent of eighteen months' salary, $43,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is the supplementary item I mentioned a moment ago, in order to provide compensation to the members of the pension appeal court which is being abolished.
How are these payments to be divided?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have already explained that, but I know my hon. friend was busy elsewhere. It is proposed to pay to the members of the pension appeal court, which will be defunct after July 1, eighteen months' salary by way of compensation.

Are all the members of the appeal court in the same position? I understand some of them have only a year and a half of their terms still to run, while others have a far longer time. It may be that the payment of eighteen months' salary to those whose terms expire in a year and a half is quite proper, but it does seem that some better provision should be made for those whose terms have several years to run. After all, these men have given up their other occupations to come here, and are now faced with the necessity of starting over again, so I think some consideration should be given to the length of time their terms have to run.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend would have been quite willing for me to abolish this court out of hand about this time last year without allowing any compensation at all.

I did not say that. The minister is going too far in making a statement of that kind. I thought the court should be done away with, but I made no personal attack of any kind on the members of the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I did not hear a good word for this court spoken by anyone in this house. The reason why I would not abolish it last year, and I so declared, was that I wanted to find some way of providing compensation for these men before turning them out on the street. Hardly a member of this house who spoke on the matter did not have something to say about me because I would not immediately, without regard to the consequences, abolish this court. They did not care what I did in the way of giving these people justice.
With respect to the one man to whom my hon. friend refers, there are two ways of looking at this question. Are we to give higher compensation to the man who served the longer time or to the man who has a longer time to serve? Frankly I do not know

whether the man who has served five years and who receives eighteen months' salary by way of compensation is any more entitled to that than the man who has served eight and a half years and who gets the same compensation. Usually we consider that the longer the term of service the greater should be the reward, and it would appear to me that in this, as in every other normal case, salary for a year and a half, amounting to approximately $10,000, is a fairly reasonable amount to pay to those who are being retired. I do not think I could be reasonably asked, or the country could be asked, to pay any more.

Personally I certainly have not recanted the position I have taken in the committee for the last three years. With regard to how much they should be given, if it were possible to make it fifty cents, still it would be an over-payment.

I wish to dissociate myself entirely from remarks such as those just made by the last speaker, which I do not think are fair in any sense of the word. I believe the minister is looking at the matter from the wrong point of view. These men were appointed for a certain term of years; they came here on the understanding that they would be retained in employment for a certain length of time. I think that should be borne in mind when compensation is being granted. The same thing would apply if a firm hired a man for a set period of time. He would have a claim against the company if he were dismissed before that time expired. I suggest to the minister that the matter should be looked at from that point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have an excellent precedent in the abolition of the pension tribunal by the former government, which allotted about this amount, or probably a little less than a year and a half salary.
Did the terms of the members of that tribunal all expire at the same time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think approximately at the same time.
That is not this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What difference does it make if a year and a half salary is reasonable? Does it make any difference when the term expires? Does my hon. friend want me to pay to the man whom he has in mind, to the friend whom he has in mind, five years' salary which would amount to $35,000?

The minister should be fair. I am not referring to any friend of mine;
I am simply asking that the matter be dealt

Central Mortgage Bank
with in a fair way. It is not a question of friendship or anything of that type.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There are four men. One man, Mr. Sherwood, is being paid his salary up to the end of his term. Another man, Mr. Justice Hyndman, is being paid his salary up to the end of his term. The third man is a civil servant; he is receiving a year and a half salary and will obtain superannuation. The fourth man, whom my hon. friend has in mind, has four to five years more to run.
I had in mind the third and fourth men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is the situation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.
Go on.
I submit that we must either obey the rules or else know the reason why.
We started at eleven o'clock this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am not insisting on proceeding. I think the committee has done remarkably well as far as I am concerned.
Progress reported.
